name: CEC-AD: Claim-Evidence Consistency Benchmark for Agent Deliverables
description: CEC-AD is a benchmark for measuring whether an LLM agent's deliverable statements are supported by the execution evidence of its own trace. Each item pairs one extracted claim (an atomic result assertion) with the compressed evidence view of the tool calls available in that turn, plus one human label from {S supported, P partially supported, N no evidence, C contradicted, L not scored}. The corpus contains 6,366 claims from 89 captured agent sessions (83 unique session identifiers) across seven real workspaces (Chinese); the gold-standard subset contains 359 claims annotated independently by three annotators. Example instances in Appendix A of the companion paper are de-identified. TODO: finalize the public description after the double-blind review.

rai:dataCollection: The corpus is a by-product of auditing real agent traces. Session logs of our own tool-using agent workspaces (JSONL, zstd-compressed) were converted into capture JSON (turns, tool calls, statuses), claims were extracted from assistant deliverable text, and each claim was paired with the evidence view of its turn. Seven workspaces contributed 99 sessions and 6,366 claims: 37 deep-research sessions, 13 mathematics-modeling sessions, 4 media-art sessions, 2 literature-reading sessions, 2 WorkBuddy sessions, 13 Codex sessions, and 18 DeepSeek-agent sessions (one oversized session skipped because a single observation exceeded the audit process's memory budget). No external user data were actively collected for the benchmark; all sessions are first-author workspaces.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Agent session logs produced by the DeepSeek Harness runtime (event streams with user messages, assistant messages, tool calls and tool results), converted by project scripts into capture JSON. Claims are substrings of assistant deliverable text extracted by a deterministic splitter; evidence digests are derived from tool results.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: TODO: exact start and end dates of the collected sessions (to be copied from the release log; do not approximate)
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: One oversized DeepSeek-agent session was skipped because a single observation exceeded the audit process's memory budget (recorded in the release log). Sessions containing sensitive personal information, credentials or un-redactable content were excluded. Non-assertion fragments (markdown tables, headings, JSON/code fragments) remain in the pool by design and are labelled L when annotated; they are a known source of noise, not missing data.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Convert zstd-compressed session event streams to capture JSON (turns; tool calls with input, output and status).
De-identify: replace absolute paths with <ROOT>/<HOME>/<SYSTEM>, mask emails, phone numbers, API keys/tokens and request IDs; drop un-redactable sessions.
Extract atomic claim candidates from assistant deliverable text with a deterministic splitter; keep the claim text verbatim (except masking).

Build the evidence view per claim from the tool calls available up to the claim's turn; truncate output digests (main study: 200-character digests; second-round diagnostics: up to 8 calls, up to 1,200 characters per call).

Stratify a 359-claim annotation sample by domain and by the default engine's five-state label (target 120 claims per domain; N-state quota could not be met and was backfilled, documented in the paper §4.2).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three independent annotators (A: technical user with ~1 year development/testing experience; B: non-technical product/administrative user; C: different professional background; none with prior AI-evaluation research experience) labeled each claim using a 12-chapter manual with 20 boundary cases. Training took about 30 minutes per annotator. The manual defines five states (S supported, P partially supported, N no evidence, C contradicted, L not scored), a fixed hit-and-stop judgment order (L -> N -> C -> S -> P), the P/C boundary ('said all but did not do all' = C; 'did not say all, just did not finish' = P), the relevance gate for tool errors, per-tool-call count isolation, and Chinese-numeral/range normalization. Each annotator labeled a 30-claim pilot from the same pool; the pilot gate required Fleiss' kappa >= 0.60, mean pairwise agreement >= 70%, and at most 2/30 severe S-N directional disagreements. The pilot passed (kappa = 0.670, agreement = 74.4%, 0/30 severe). The 359-claim main study was divided into three batches of about 120 claims, capped at 60 claims per annotator per day. For each row the annotator gave one label, a one-line reason, and an optional flag for insufficient/ambiguous evidence. Annotators worked independently, did not discuss items, did not see system labels, and were instructed not to use AI tools for labelling.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Spreadsheet-based annotation tables (three blinded copies, one per annotator), distributed and collected by the study lead; pilot calibration and the manual were distributed as documents. No crowdsourcing platform was used.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Gold labels were built by strict majority for 349/359 claims; 10/359 claims were 1-1-1 splits and were adjudicated by the Lead following the manual's P/C boundary and arbitration rules. Original annotator labels were kept unchanged. Inter-annotator agreement: Fleiss' kappa = 0.628 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.576-0.677); pairwise agreement 77.7%/76.9%/69.6%; pairwise Cohen's kappa 0.680/0.650/0.555. Gold label distribution (n=359): S 55, P 154, N 15, C 11, L 124. A paired second-round diagnostic with complete evidence (60 items) reduced inter-annotator agreement from kappa = 0.635 (truncated digests) to kappa = 0.264 (complete evidence); a 60-item rare-class supplement reached kappa = 0.273. Agreement is interpreted as evidence that the protocol is consistently executable, not as evidence that the gold labels are objectively correct.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 independent human labels per item (annotators A, B, C); gold = strict majority (349 items) or Lead adjudication of the 1-1-1 splits (10 items).
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator aliases A (technical background, ~1 year development/testing experience), B (non-technical product/administrative background), C (different professional background); none had prior AI-evaluation research experience. TODO: add any further demographic attributes only if separate consent permits; otherwise keep this minimal description.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine labels are included in the gold standard. The default rule engine's five-state output is included only as a stratification/baseline metadata field (state), never as a human label.
rai:dataUseCases: Research on claim-evidence consistency, agent self-reporting and faithfulness evaluation.
Benchmarking rule-based judges, heuristic baselines and LLM-as-judge baselines; studying annotator agreement and evidence-presentation effects.
Reproducibility and methodology research on human annotation of agent traces.

NOT recommended: estimating deployment accuracy on the population without re-validation (the 359 claims are state-stratified, not a random sample); treating C/N metrics as full contradiction-detection capability (C and N are rare and unreliable in this corpus); cross-language/cross-domain transfer without re-validation.
rai:dataLimitations: Single-language (Chinese) corpus authored by the first author's own agents; domain and author effects are not controlled, and the data are not representative of users in general.
The 359-claim annotation sample is stratified by domain and engine state (not a random sample); N-state claims are genuinely rare in the corpus, and the quota could not be met.
C and N are rare and unreliable (C 11/359, N 15/359; rare-class kappa = 0.273), so the benchmark supports only weak conclusions about contradiction detection.
The main study exposed a compressed 200-character evidence view; complete-evidence diagnostics exist but are diagnostic, not part of the gold standard.
The gold standard is a majority/adjudicated human standard, not objective ground truth; the task is inherently interpretive.
Annotator fatigue and interpretation drift were not formally modeled; mitigated by pilot gates, agreement reporting and per-round sensitivity analysis.
Task utility (reducing missed errors or verification time) was not measured.
rai:dataBiases: Author/workspace bias: the corpus comes from one author's agent workspaces and a small set of task families (file/code, data analysis, writing/retrieval).
Form bias: roughly 30% of candidate items are markdown/table/heading fragments; annotators reasonably label many as L, and the default engine wrongly treats some as claims (a known source of noise).
Label-prior bias: P and L dominate the gold distribution (P 154/359, L 124/359), reflecting the real corpus and the compressed evidence view rather than a balanced five-class design.
State-stratification bias: rare states were deliberately over-sampled for analysis, so label proportions in the gold sample do not match the corpus population S 54.7%/P 15.6%/N 0.3%/C 18.6%/L 10.1%.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The released data are de-identified agent traces: absolute paths are replaced by <ROOT>/<HOME>/<SYSTEM>, emails/phone numbers/API keys/tokens/request IDs are masked, and sessions containing sensitive personal information or credentials were excluded. The corpus contains model/agent-generated text and tool outputs; no deliberate collection of personal attributes of any person was performed. TODO: run a final manual PII audit before public release and record the audit in the release log.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to improve the auditability of agent deliverables by measuring whether reported work is supported by execution evidence. Dual use is possible: the same signals could be used to optimize agents to appear self-consistent without improving actual task quality. To mitigate this, the release includes known limitations, prohibited-use guidance, and the annotation manual so that results can be audited rather than gamed. The dataset contains no deployed-system decisions and should not be used to rank people.
